units.title: Third-person -s / -es
units.rule: In the present simple, add -s or -es after he, she, it or a singular subject. Change consonant + y to -ies.
units.example: She reads. He watches. My sister studies.

units.title: Base verbs after auxiliaries
units.rule: After do, does, did, do not, does not or did not, use the base form of the main verb.
units.example: Does she play? He does not play. Did they go?

units.title: Forms of be
units.rule: Match be to the subject and time: I am; he/she/it is; we/you/they are. In the past, use was with I/he/she/it and were with we/you/they.
units.example: I am ready. They are ready. We were tired yesterday.

units.title: Have, has and there is / are
units.rule: Use has with he/she/it or a singular subject; use have with I/you/we/they. Use there is for one thing and there are for more than one.
units.example: She has a notebook. They have notebooks. There are two books.

units.title: Completed past actions
units.rule: Use the past simple for completed actions at a past time. Regular verbs end in -ed; some verbs have irregular past forms.
units.example: We visited the museum yesterday. She went home.

units.title: Actions happening now
units.rule: For an action happening now, use am/is/are + verb-ing. Match the auxiliary to the subject.
units.example: I am reading. She is writing. They are playing.

units.title: Actions in progress in the past
units.rule: Use was/were + verb-ing for an action in progress at a past moment. A shorter event can interrupt it.
units.example: I was reading when the phone rang.

units.title: Experience and recent results
units.rule: Use have/has + past participle for experiences or past actions linked to now. Words such as ever, never, just, already and yet often help.
units.example: I have seen this film. She has just arrived.

units.title: Make and do
units.rule: Learn these combinations as whole phrases: do homework, do your best, make a decision, make a mistake, make your bed and make friends.
units.example: Do your homework. Make a decision.

units.title: Take and get
units.rule: Learn action phrases together: take a photo, take a break, take notes, take part and get enough sleep.
units.example: Take a photo. Get enough sleep.

units.title: Communication phrases
units.rule: Use tell the truth, ask a question, give advice, send an email, pay attention and keep a promise.
units.example: Ask a question. Give advice. Tell the truth.

units.title: Study and everyday phrases
units.rule: Learn common combinations: solve a problem, follow the rules, save money, protect the environment and win a match.
units.example: Solve a problem. Follow the rules.

units.title: At, on and in for time
units.rule: Use at with clock times, on with days and dates, and in with months and years. Learn at night and in the morning as phrases.
units.example: At nine. On Monday. In September.

units.title: Place and movement
units.rule: Use in for something inside, on for a surface, to for a destination and across for movement from one side to the other. Learn arrive at a place and arrive in a city or country.
units.example: In a bag. On a wall. Walk across a bridge.

units.title: Prepositions in fixed phrases
units.rule: Learn the preposition with its phrase: good at, interested in, afraid of, listen to, wait for, agree with and belong to.
units.example: Good at maths. Interested in science.

units.title: For and since
units.rule: Use for with a length of time and since with the point when something began.
units.example: For three years. Since 2020.

units.title: Statements and noun phrases
units.rule: In a simple statement, put the subject before the verb, then the object. Put an adjective before the noun it describes.
units.example: She reads books. I have a blue bag.

units.title: Question word order
units.rule: In questions, put the auxiliary before the subject. With a question word, use question word + auxiliary + subject + main verb.
units.example: Where does she live? Did you see it?

units.title: Frequency adverbs
units.rule: Frequency adverbs usually come before a main verb and after be. Keep noun phrases together.
units.example: She often reads. He is always polite.

units.title: Auxiliaries and verb groups
units.rule: Keep auxiliaries and main verbs in order. Use subject + modal + base verb, have/has + past participle, or be + going to + base verb.
units.example: She can swim. He has just arrived.

units.title: Common word spellings
units.rule: Check the whole word, not only how it sounds. Notice the letter sequence in because, beautiful, science, subject and information.
units.example: because · beautiful · science

units.title: Single and double letters
units.rule: Notice which consonants are doubled: address has dd and ss; tomorrow has rr; necessary has one c and two s.
units.example: address · tomorrow · necessary

units.title: Silent letters and letter order
units.rule: Some letters are written but not heard. Check listen, answer and Wednesday. In friend, i comes before e.
units.example: listen · answer · Wednesday · friend

units.title: Capital letters
units.rule: Use capitals for I, names, languages, countries, months and days. Begin a sentence with a capital letter.
units.example: I study English in Kazakhstan on Monday.
